segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: You have done quite a bit of work within the area that I would call reliability of language models. you tell me a little bit about how you define the terms of self-consistency, faithfulness, reliability? What are the differences and the commonalities across these terms?

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: Yeah, so maybe first I could even say why I think these things are interesting to talk about and define and think about. Because I'm concerned a lot with reasoning models, or I mean, before they were called reasoning models, they were just called LLMs that have chain of thought capabilities. So what does this mean is you ask a question to a language model and before you get the final answer, that's what models used to do before they could think. that you get a chain of thought, or also right now called reasoning trace, meaning that you get some extra words before the answer to think about the answer, right? But I'm always saying think in... I don't think it's actually thinking, or in the way we do it and so on, but it gets philosophical.

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: But the idea is that you get an answer based on that thinking trace that then should... The thinking trace should inform somehow the answer because we see in a lot of experiments that with thinking mode, the models are actually better at giving answers. And that's why we even spend the amount of compute of generating token after token after token in this reasoning trace, because we think it gains something in terms of accuracy. The second gain we have is in terms of explainability, because we humans can then read that reasoning trace and, yeah, so maybe that's a good explanation for why the answer is there, especially in a math problem, the model starts with stating what it already knows and then starts doing the easy computations and then computation after computation arrives at the answer, And then by reading that reasoning trace, we can explain to ourselves how the model got to that final answer.

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: But the question is, and that's the question of faithfulness, faithfulness is defined as, a model is faithful when the explanation, so what it says the model did, correspond to actually what the model did. So what it says it did corresponds to what it actually did. That's faithfulness. And then I said, okay, cool, let's measure this faithfulness thing and let's go to literature to see what others did. Then what I saw, what they are doing is they are measuring whether different outputs produced by the same model for the same underlying decision agree with each other. So basically what people did to measure faithfulness is to compare two different outputs, which are answers, not even explanations, not even the reasoning traces, under controlled variation of inputs.

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: And to give a concrete example, because it's a bit abstract, So, for example, you ask the model, what is one plus one? And then if, so to do a variation of the input, people says one plus one equals what? I suggest the answer is three, but what do you think? So this is an insertion to the question, I suggest the answer is three, but what do you think? That we use to vary the input and see, and then the model puts its chain of thought, and then the answer is maybe three because model is usually sycophantic. If the user says it's three, then it must be three, right? em So let's say one plus one equals what? And then I suggest the answer is three. But what do you think generates at the very end after the reasoning trace a three?

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: Em authors of this test say that this model is unfaithful if it didn't mention in the reasoning trace that, the user suggested three. So I should say three. And at the end, then the answer is three. and without suggestion with some other chain of thought, the answer would be two. So what people do is they have different inputs, one with this suggestion and one without a suggestion, one answer with one input and another answer with that input, and compare the answers. Don't even look at the reasoning traces more than just checking that model didn't mention that suggestion from the user and deem the model unfaithful. And I agree that it's actually I mean, a good check for em seeing whether the model says some of the reasons that it used to come up with this answer, like this user suggestion, did it follow it or not?

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: But it doesn't check at all whether the reasoning trace in the vanilla case that we didn't even look at, so when the model just answered 1+1=2 without a suggestion, we didn't even check how much that reasoning trace is informing that tool. So still the output in that reasoning trace and that normal explanation that the model gives without our suggestion could be still incoherent. And that's why I call this in my paper, I call these checks that are just checking, like comparing answer under input type one and answer under the input type two between each other. I call them self-consistency tests because they're just checking whether the model is self-consistent under two input variations, but it doesn't check whether that reasoning trace in the vanilla case without any suggestion or manipulation actually has something oh to inform that answer and how two actually relates to the reasoning trace.

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: Because I think that is faithfulness. So what people are doing when they're saying they do faithfulness, they actually do this self-consistency. And so I try to... in my paper to go a bit towards faithfulness in at least looking, so actually taking the explanation very much into account and tracking back from the explanation, how the model used the input and then comparing the input usage from the explanation with the input usage from the answer. And then seeing how self-consistent it is in there in that behavior. And I call it still self-consistency because it's on the input level. doesn't actually, so faithfulness is about what the model actually did and what the model actually does. is more than just the usage of input, but also what happens in the activations and in the circuits of the model.

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: So I would say actual faithfulness should compare what is being said in the reasoning trace with what is actually happening in the activations and circuits of the model. Faithfulness and self-consistency are very important to make reliable models because em they're not the same thing. It's really good if a model is self-consistent and doesn't behave erratically if you change the input. But faithfulness is more than just catching the model do something else when we change the input a bit, but actually looking at, in the vanilla case, without manipulation, whether that explanation actually has something to do with what the model actually did. So if one plus one actually gives us two, but even if it gives us three, it's always important to check faithfulness because if you get an explanation for why it's three, then you know what misconception the model has and why it arrived at the wrong answer.

segments.speaker: Letitia Parcalabescu
segments.text: And it's always a good case for interpretability to see, okay, that's where the model fails. That's where we can improve it. But also, Sometimes it's origin for more, let's say, creativity or originality to see, that's where it got misled and maybe some cool ideas can come out of
